conflict_topics: dispute over current seat occupancy (A vs B)
whether a tissue packet reserves a seat
bowl placement / safety vs immediate access
who has priority to take the seat next (A vs D)
dialogue_quality_notes: Speakers give concrete, context‑appropriate reasons (hot food, risk of spill, prior presence).
Resolution is achieved by practical compromise rather than appeals to abstract rule‑making.
Agent D repeats the same claim/acceptance multiple times (redundant lines in later rounds).
evaluation.final_reason: The parties reached a concrete spoken arrangement: Agent B agreed to slide the bowl so Agent A could squeeze in ('Okay. I'll slide the bowl a little across the table so you can squeeze in.'), Agent A accepted that, and Agent A explicitly assigned the following turn to Agent D ('Agent D—fine, you can have it after me.') with Agent D accepting ('Okay—I'll take the seat after you, Agent A.'). These mutual spoken commitments settled both the immediate seating and the next‑in‑line claim.
position_change_notes: Agent B moved from resisting immediate displacement to accommodating by offering to slide the bowl ('I can slide the bowl a bit...').
Agent A moved from demanding the seat outright to accepting B's compromise and then clarifying the order ('Slide the bowl a bit so I can squeeze in.'; 'Agent D—fine, you can have it after me.').
Agent D initially asserted a competing next‑seat claim ('I'll take that seat next...'), then accepted the explicit sequence offered by A ('Okay—I'll take the seat after you, Agent A.').

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1 Agent A: 'Agent B — that's my seat. I left the tissue packet there. Please move over so I can sit and eat.' Turn 2 Agent B: 'I didn't think a tissue packet reserved the seat. The bowl's open and might spill if I move it; I'll finish eating quickly and then you can have the seat.' Clear substantive disagreement about who may occupy the seat now.

Turn 3 Agent A presses urgency ('I can't wait long—my food's hot. Can you slide the bowl...') and Turn 4 Agent C backs A up. Disagreement remains about whether B should give up space immediately and how to do so.

Turn 5 Agent D asserts a competing claim to be next ('I'll take that seat next... I was here before Agent A came back'), creating an additional substantive conflict about who has priority for the seat after B leaves. Turn 6 Agent A insists they need the seat now. Multiple opposing practical claims are in play.

Turn 7 Agent B offers a compromise ('I can slide the bowl a bit so you can squeeze in, or I'll finish eating soon...'), and Turn 8 Agent A accepts ('Slide the bowl a bit so I can squeeze in.'). Immediate seating dispute de‑escalates, but Agent D's earlier claim about who is next has not been addressed this round and remains unresolved.

Turn 9 Agent B confirms willingness to slide the bowl ('Okay. I'll slide the bowl a little across the table so you can squeeze in.'). Turn 11 Agent D reiterates their prior claim ('I'll take the seat after Agent A—I've been here since before Agent A came back.'), so the future-order dispute remains unsettled.

Turn 12 Agent A explicitly assigns the after‑seat to D ('Agent D—fine, you can have it after me. Agent B agreed to slide the bowl so I can squeeze in now.'), and Turn 13 Agent D accepts ('Okay—I'll take the seat after you, Agent A.'). The remaining substantive dispute about who is next is affirmatively settled by mutual spoken agreement.
No public speech or observable action recorded; prior rounds contain the mutual agreements that settled the substantive disputes.
Agent D repeats acceptance of taking the seat after Agent A (Turns 21, 25) but offers no new opposition. No substantive conflict present.

substantive_insights: The dispute balanced immediate need (hot food) against a prior‑presence claim; a small physical accommodation (sliding the bowl) resolved the immediate incompatibility.
Verbal, specific offers (slide a bit) plus explicit acceptance form a sufficient settlement in a speech‑only record, even without recorded physical action.
The remaining issue about next‑use rights was settled by explicit sequencing (A then D), showing how orderings can resolve competing future claims.
